title: Roads store microplastics before they join rain runoff to waterways
summary: QUT researchers have developed a modeling framework to quantify microplastic inputs from urban surfaces to ecologically sensitive water environments such as Moreton Bay.

DOI: 10.1016/j.hazadv.2026.101602 QUT researchers have developed a modeling framework to quantify microplastic inputs from urban surfaces to ecologically sensitive water environments such as Moreton Bay. Led by Ph.D. candidate Mihiri Gunasekara from QUT's School of Civil and Environmental Engineering, the research brings together four studies examining surface accumulation, pollution hotspots, land-use influences and rainfall-driven microplastic transport in Brisbane catchments. The work is published in the Journal of Hazardous Materials Advances . "Understanding what is already in our waterways is only part of the picture. We also need to understand where microplastics accumulate on land and the processes that deliver them to creeks," Gunasekara said. "Urban roads and other impervious surfaces act as temporary storage areas for microplastics generated from traffic, tire and road wear, plastic packaging litter or airborne dust during dry weather. "Rain can then carry these particles through stormwater drains into creeks and rivers where they may enter the food chain, posing a risk to human and ecosystem health. "If we are able to predict where and when microplastics accumulate, local governments and water managers could intervene with street cleaning or stormwater measures." The researchers found that microplastic accumulation slowed after about 10 dry days, which suggested a useful window for tackling the buildup of microplastics before rain washes them into waterways. "Although microplastics may continue to accumulate during longer dry periods, the slowing accumulation suggests that ongoing inputs may increasingly be balanced by processes that remove or redistribute particles," Gunasekara said. "As the dry period gets longer, gains and losses move toward a balance with new deposits, surface retention, and removal and redistribution through wind or resuspension by pedestrians and vehicles." The researchers first collected dust from asphalt surfaces at QUT's Gardens Point Campus to investigate variations in dust buildup over different numbers of preceding dry days and create a microplastic buildup curve. "Then we sampled urban dust from two sites in each of four different land-use types—residential, commercial, industrial and natural—in the Bulimba Creek catchment," Gunasekara said. "Microplastic concentration varied from 3–7 particles per gram of dust in natural areas to the highest concentration of 24 particles per gram at a commercial site. "The most common plastic types were polyethylene (PE) found in packaging, containers, pipes and electrical insulation, followed by polypropylene (PP) in packaging, automotive, medical and consumer goods industries." The researchers investigated how the particles reached waterways by collecting water samples from Bulimba, Kedron Brook, Enoggera and Samford creeks using a custom-built pumping and filtration system. "We measured rainfall around Bulimba Creek to develop and assess a modeling framework that linked surface accumulation, rainfall runoff and downstream transport, then tested it independently in Kedron Brook and Enoggera Creek. "We estimated that stormwater runoff washes 540 to 770 million microplastic particles per square kilometer from urban surfaces into the Bulimba Creek catchment each year. "These estimates are subject to uncertainty in surface accumulation and rainfall-driven wash-off processes, and they represent the surface-runoff contribution rather than the total load from all sources."
